extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students and general readers studying American government, public policy, and state social/economic legislation
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptions of state-level legal standards and administrative duties across labor relations, public health, charities, education, morals, and selected constitutional provisions. Summarizes statutory powers, duties, definitions, and institutional arrangements used to regulate these social and economic areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission requirements to state board of mediation and arbitration
rubrics_metrics.description: Any grievance or dispute between an employer and his employees may be submitted to this board for determination and settlement. Such submission must be in writing and contain a detailed statement of the dispute and its causes, and also an agreement to abide by the determination of the board and to continue at business or work during the investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Upon submission the board must hear testimony and investigate the matter and, within ten days after completion of the hearing, render a decision, a copy of which is to be served upon each party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandate on prompt local mediation by bureau representative
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever a strike or lockout occurs or is seriously threatened, a representative of the bureau shall, if practicable, proceed to the locality promptly and endeavor to effect an amicable settlement by way of mediation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended to prevent escalation by timely intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: State boards' power to initiate investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: In several states boards of mediation and arbitration may on their own initiative investigate the causes of industrial disputes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arbitration has not been made obligatory upon employers and employees; boards can still proactively investigate and attempt conciliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical functions and limits of conciliation/ arbitration boards
rubrics_metrics.description: A board with power to intervene instantly may sometimes effect settlement by bringing parties together and suggesting bases of agreement; failing that, publishing findings and indicating a fair settlement may produce public pressure for compromise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although without power to enforce awards, publicizing findings and timely suggestion of compromises can often prevent strikes and lockouts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powers and duties of state commissioner/department of public health
rubrics_metrics.description: The commissioner is charged with taking cognizance of the interests of health and life of the people and all matters appertaining thereto; he makes inquiries into causes of diseases; investigates sources of mortality; studies effects of localities, employments, and other conditions upon health; obtains and preserves information useful to promotion of health and security of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He may compel attendance of witnesses and force them to testify; may reverse local board regulations under certain circumstances; on governor's order must make examinations and, on report discovering a public nuisance, the governor may order it abated or removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health code prohibition and definition of adulterated foods and drugs
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete public health code will forbid the manufacture and sale of adulterated foods and drugs. Food is adulterated if any substance has been mixed so as to reduce, lower, or injuriously affect its quality or strength; if inferior or cheaper substances have been substituted wholly or in part; if any valuable constituent has been wholly or partly abstracted; if the article is an imitation or sold under the name of another substance; or if it contains diseased or decomposed animal or vegetable substances, or, in the case of milk foods, is a product of diseased animals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most health laws further provide for maintaining certain standards in drugs and for a certain degree of purity in liquors and confectionery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspection and sanitary regulation of potable water and ports
rubrics_metrics.description: Health law provides for inspection of all potable waters in the state to prevent contamination from sewage and other sources; it creates a quarantine and a health officer at the port of New York.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the health department's preventive and regulatory duties to protect public water supplies and control infectious disease entry via ports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation of medical and allied professions and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Health law regulates the practice of medicine, dentistry, veterinary medicine, and surgery; provides for registration and regulation of pharmacies and drug stores; supervises chiropody, undertaking and embalming, and optometry; provides for vaccination of school children; and visitation of institutions for orphans, destitute, vagrant children, or juvenile delinquents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad supervisory authority intended to ensure professional standards and institutional oversight affecting public health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenement-house law standards
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-developed tenement-house law will require certain precautions against fire through regulations relative to the construction of halls, stairways, and fire-escapes; it will define the percentage of a lot which may be occupied by buildings and define the minimum of light and ventilation. Example: New York prescribes minimum window area for each room in new tenement-houses and minimum room sizes; it regulates sanitary accommodations and penalizes landlords who neglect property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Right to commence new buildings and to alter structures in large cities is subjected to control by tenement-house or health department.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspection and supervision duties of state board of charities
rubrics_metrics.description: State board of charities is required to visit, inspect, and maintain a general supervision over all institutions, state and municipal, of a charitable, correctional, or reformatory character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board must aid in securing just, humane, and economic administration of institutions; advise officers; secure suitable accommodations for inmates; control organization and incorporation of new charitable and reformatory institutions; and assist in maintaining high standards of efficient and humane service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local responsibility for care of the poor
rubrics_metrics.description: Care of the poor (persons unable to maintain themselves) is generally vested under state laws in county or town authorities; the local body usually provides poorhouses and institutions under the care of a superintendent or overseer of the poor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflects devolved local administration of public relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education as a state and local function
rubrics_metrics.description: Education in the United States is regarded as a purely state and local function; the federal bureau of education has no administrative control over state systems and is limited to study and publication of educational data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State autonomy produces adaptability to local needs but resists national control of curricula/administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional mandates for free common schools and compulsory attendance
rubrics_metrics.description: Many state constitutions embody the principle that knowledge diffused through the community is essential and require the legislature to provide for maintenance and support of a system of free common schools. Some constitutions go farther and provide for compulsory attendance—e.g., Oklahoma requires attendance of children aged eight to sixteen (sound in mind and body) unless other education provided, fixing minimum education at three months each year; Nebraska requires free instruction to persons between ages five and twenty-one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate constitutional-level requirements that shape state statutory education systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: State constitutional provision for higher education institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: A number of state constitutions set aside provisions for a state university or require the legislature to encourage moral, intellectual, scientific, and agricultural improvement; some constitutions provide for a complete and uniform system of public instruction including universities and technical/professional departments (example: Wyoming).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides constitutional authorization and limits for state involvement in higher education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special funds and revenue sources for education
rubrics_metrics.description: Some state constitutions set aside special funds for educational purposes—e.g., Nebraska declares perpetual funds for common schools from amounts granted by Congress on sale of lands, proceeds of sections sixteen and thirty-six, proceeds of escheat/forfeiture, fines, penalties, license moneys, and other specified revenues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies stable funding sources enshrined constitutionally for education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on public aid to denominational schools
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally the constitution stipulates that neither the state nor any subdivision may allow use of its property, credit, or public money, directly or indirectly, in aiding and maintaining any school or institution of learning under control of any religious denomination (except for examination and inspection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes separation of public funds from sectarian education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties and limited powers of state superintendent/commissioner of education
rubrics_metrics.description: State superintendent's duties usually include visiting the state, cooperating with county superintendents and local authorities to develop uniformly higher standards, collecting statistics and data, devising plans for improvement, and reporting to the governor and legislature; often supervises normal schools but has little power to prescribe subjects or methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Role is largely advisory, statistical, and promotional rather than commanding classroom practice in most states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation in powers of central boards of education
rubrics_metrics.description: Central boards of education vary from being guardians of school funds and lands, to advisory bodies to the superintendent, to boards with large authority over the whole state system including making rules affecting curriculum, books, methods of instruction, examinations, and appointment of teachers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extent of centralization differs by state; legislature enacts the laws upon which systems rest.

rubrics_metrics.name: State responsibility for establishing/maintaining universities and granting degrees
rubrics_metrics.description: The central government of the state controls incorporation of colleges and institutions of higher education; it is from the state that institutions secure power to grant degrees and the state commonly establishes and maintains state universities and normal schools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State acts as the legal and financial backbone of public higher education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universities' extension of services beyond classical curricula
rubrics_metrics.description: State universities are becoming more public-service oriented: founding extension departments, correspondence schools, short courses (e.g., for farmers), centers throughout the state, and sending lecturers to deliver cultural and practical courses; universities widen curriculum to include technology, engineering, agriculture, and domestic science and conduct applied laboratory research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasis on widening access and practical application of university research for state economic and social needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local administrative organization of schools and districts
rubrics_metrics.description: Administration of education is for the most part local: counties, cities, townships have superintendents, boards of education, or trustees; townships are often the lowest administrative division; school districts are formed usually without crossing township lines and have boards or single officers elected locally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local electoral or appointive mechanisms determine school governance in many places (exceptions in New England noted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of traveling libraries and extension systems to broaden education
rubrics_metrics.description: States have established public libraries, travelling libraries, and extension systems to carry education beyond school limits—e.g., Indiana's travelling libraries circulate small boxes of books on special subjects through local associations at nominal cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical program example: nearly two hundred travelling libraries containing about six thousand books circulated by 1907 in Indiana.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws regulating public morals and Sunday observance
rubrics_metrics.description: Common practice to prohibit labor on Sunday except works of necessity and charity and to forbid public sports, exercises, shows, and noises disturbing the public peace on Sunday.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of state moral regulation intersecting with public order and custom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibitions and regulation of gambling and tobacco
rubrics_metrics.description: Gambling, pool selling, lotteries, and betting on races are generally forbidden; a number of states have attempted to limit manufacture and sale of cigarettes (example: Indiana made it unlawful).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States exercise police power to restrict activities deemed morally or socially harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation and prohibition of intoxicating liquors, and local option
rubrics_metrics.description: The manufacture and sale of intoxicating liquors are placed under strict supervision and in a number of cases entirely prohibited. Many states adopted prohibition historically; later shifts included high license systems and wide use of 'local option' laws allowing counties, townships, villages, or cities to abolish sale of liquor by popular vote or petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By 1909 two-thirds of territory and almost one-half of people were under prohibition laws; local option produces gradual regional change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article I — Vesting of legislative powers in Congress
rubrics_metrics.description: All legislative powers herein granted shall be vested in a Congress of the United States, which shall consist of a Senate and House of Representatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional structural rule establishing bicameral federal legislature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article I — House of Representatives composition and qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: The House shall be composed of members chosen every second year by the people of the several states; no person shall be a representative who shall not have attained to the age of twenty-five years, and been seven years a citizen of the United States, and who shall not, when elected, be an inhabitant of that state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also contains apportionment rules (enumeration every ten years, three-fifths clause for 'other persons' at the time) and limits on representative-to-population ratio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article I — House powers regarding officers and impeachment
rubrics_metrics.description: The House of Representatives shall choose their speaker and other officers; and shall have the sole power of impeachment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocates internal organizational authority and the initial impeachment function to the House.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article I — Senate composition, classes, vacancies, and qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: The Senate shall be composed of two senators from each state, chosen by the legislature thereof, for six years; they shall be divided into three classes so that one third may be chosen every second year; executive of a state may make temporary appointments to fill vacancies during the recess until the legislature meets to fill vacancies. No person shall be a senator who shall not have attained to the age of thirty years and been nine years a citizen and an inhabitant when elected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescribes staggered terms, vacancy-filling procedures, and age/citizenship/inhabitancy qualifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article I — Vice President and Senate officers; impeachment trial rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The Vice President shall be President of the Senate but have no vote unless equally divided; the Senate chooses other officers and a president pro tempore; the Senate shall have the sole power to try all impeachments, sitting on oath or affirmation; when the President is tried the chief justice shall preside; conviction requires concurrence of two thirds of members present; judgment in cases of impeachment shall not extend further than removal and disqualification though convicted party remains liable to indictment and punishment according to law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines procedural safeguards and limits of impeachment remedies.
